name: CVD risk
seoDesc: CVD risk: work out CVD risk from the age and the HDL cholesterol. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the CVD risk calculator the age, the HDL cholesterol, the total cholesterol and the systolic blood pressure and it returns CVD risk. Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the CVD risk calculator work?
sections.html:
The CVD risk calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports CVD risk in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the sex); then you type in the age, the HDL cholesterol, the total cholesterol and the systolic blood pressure.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as female and male. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in years. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in milligrams per deciliter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 2 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in milligrams per deciliter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 2 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in millimeters of mercury. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “I am being treated for hypertension”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “I am a smoker”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “I have diabetes”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.

4 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the CVD risk calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

CVD risk=(sex, age) + (diabetes VS, sex) + (HDL cholesterol) + (systolic blood pressure, hypertension VS, sex) + (smoker VS, sex) + (total cholesterol, sex)
10-year risk of cardiovascular disease=(1 ÷ 100) × ((sex, age) + (diabetes VS, sex) + (HDL cholesterol) + (systolic blood pressure, hypertension VS, sex) + (smoker VS, sex) + (total cholesterol, sex), sex)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.
  • Shown in percent, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Time, opening in years
  • Cholesterol – for HDL or LDL, opening in milligrams per deciliter
  • Cholesterol – for HDL or LDL, opening in milligrams per deciliter
  • Pressure, opening in millimeters of mercury
  • %, opening in percent

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The CVD risk calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the age, the HDL cholesterol and the total cholesterol — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the CVD risk calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns CVD risk, derived from the age, the HDL cholesterol and the total cholesterol. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the CVD risk calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the age, the HDL cholesterol, the total cholesterol and the systolic blood pressure, which is 8 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter age in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Age opens in years and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the CVD risk calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
